title: Achaemenides. Polyphemus. Anchisae mors
titleEn: Achaemenides's Tale, Polyphemus and the Death of Anchises — Aeneid III.613–718
part: Achaemenides's Tale, Polyphemus and the Death of Anchises (III.613–718)
about: The castaway Achaemenides, a poor man's son from Ithaca who sailed to Troy with Ulysses, tells his story. His comrades fled the Cyclops's cave and forgot him; he has seen Polyphemus, huge and bloody, dash two men against the rock and chew their limbs. Ulysses did not suffer it: when the giant lay drunk and sodden with wine and flesh, the men prayed, drew lots, and bored out his single eye. Now Achaemenides urges the Trojans to cut their cables and flee, for a hundred other Cyclopes roam these mountains; he himself has lived on berries and roots for nearly three months, trembling, and gave himself up to the first ship he saw. Hardly has he finished when Polyphemus appears on the heights, leaning on a pine, his sheep, his only comfort, following him down to the sea, where he washes his bleeding eye. The Trojans take Achaemenides aboard and cut the cable in silence. The blind giant hears the oars, cannot catch them, and roars so that the sea, Italy and Etna shake; the other Cyclopes pour down to the shore, towering like oaks and cypresses, but too late. In fear the Trojans run before the wind, and the warnings of Helenus about Scylla and Charybdis turn them back; Boreas springs up from the Strait of Pelorus and carries them down the Sicilian coast. Aeneas names the places they pass: Ortygia and the spring of Arethusa, the Helorus, Pachynus, Camarina, Gela, Acragas, Selinus and Lilybaeum. At Drepanum, after so many storms, Aeneas loses his father Anchises, and he addresses him in grief: neither Helenus nor Celaeno had foretold this. With that his tale of Troy and of the wanderings ends, and the narrator closes the long story that began at the start of Book II, with Aeneas falling silent.

sentences.t:
“Sum patria ex Ithaca, comes infelicis Ulixi,
nomine Achaemenides, Troiam genitore Adamasto
paupere—mansissetque utinam fortuna!—profectus.
sentences.l:
“I am from Ithaca, my country, comrade of unlucky Ulysses,
by name Achaemenides, to Troy, my father Adamastus
poor — and would that fortune had remained! — having set out.
sentences.i: “My country is Ithaca, and I was a comrade of ill-fated Ulysses, Achaemenides by name; I set out for Troy because my father Adamastus was poor — if only my fortune had stayed as it was!
sentences.n: The part opens inside Achaemenides's speech, which Aeneas is reporting (the speech marks run from here to 654); this line also begins one of Greenough's paragraphs. 'Sum patria ex Ithaca' — 'patria' is an ablative of respect, 'Ithacan by country'. 'genitore Adamasto paupere' — an ablative absolute with no participle, 'my father Adamastus being poor', with the name in apposition. 'profectus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'proficiscor', 'having set out'. The dashes enclose a wish: 'mansissetque utinam fortuna!' is an unfulfilled wish about the past, 'utinam' with the pluperfect subjunctive ('would that fortune had remained'): his poor lot at home now looks better than what followed. Achaemenides is Virgil's own addition to the Cyclops story: in Odyssey 9 Ulysses' surviving men all get away.

sentences.t:
Hic me, dum trepidi crudelia limina linquunt,
inmemores socii vasto Cyclopis in antro
deseruere.
sentences.l:
Here me, while anxious they leave the cruel thresholds,
forgetful, my comrades in the vast Cyclops's cave
abandoned.
sentences.i: Here, while they were fleeing in terror from the cruel doorway, my comrades forgot me and left me behind in the Cyclops's vast cave.
sentences.n: 'dum… linquunt' — 'dum' with a historic present, 'while they were leaving'. 'trepidi' and 'inmemores' agree with 'socii' and give the manner of the desertion ('anxious', 'forgetful'). 'limina' is a poetic plural for one threshold. 'Cyclopis' is the genitive singular of 'Cyclops'. 'deseruere' = 'deseruerunt' (the ending '-ere' for '-erunt'; you'll see it constantly). 'hic' is the adverb 'here', pointing to the cave.

sentences.t:
Domus sanie dapibusque cruentis,
intus opaca, ingens;
sentences.l:
The house with gore and feasts bloody,
inside dark, huge;
sentences.i: His house is bloody with gore and with its horrid feasts, dark within, enormous;
sentences.n: A sentence with no verb: 'est' is understood after 'Domus', and the three descriptions pile up in short strokes. 'sanie dapibusque cruentis' — 'cruentis' is an ablative of respect or cause, 'bloody with'; 'sanie' is the ablative of 'sanies', 'gore, foul blood'. 'intus opaca' — 'intus' is an adverb, 'inside', and 'opaca' agrees with 'domus': dark within.

sentences.t:
ipse arduus, altaque pulsat
sidera—Di, talem terris avertite pestem!—
nec visu facilis nec dictu adfabilis ulli.
sentences.l:
he himself towering, and the high
stars he strikes — Gods, such a plague from the lands turn away! —
neither to see easy nor to address affable to anyone.
sentences.i: He himself is tall and strikes the lofty stars — gods, keep such a plague away from the earth! — neither pleasant to look upon nor approachable in speech by any man.
sentences.n: 'altaque… sidera' — the adjective and noun are split, with 'pulsat' between them; the hyperbole 'strikes the stars' is a stock way of saying a giant's head is in the sky (Homer compares Polyphemus to a wooded peak in Odyssey 9). 'Di' is the contracted nominative or vocative plural of 'deus' (= 'dei'); 'avertite' is an imperative, a prayer cried out in the middle of the description. 'terris' is a dative of reference with 'avertite', 'away from the lands'. 'visu' and 'dictu' are supines in the ablative (of respect: 'easy as to seeing', 'affable as to speaking'); you'll see 'dictu', 'visu', 'factu' as set phrases. 'ulli' is a dative with 'adfabilis'. 'adfabilis' is Greenough's spelling (the familiar form is 'affabilis').

sentences.t: Visceribus miserorum et sanguine vescitur atro.
sentences.l: On the entrails of wretches and on blood he feeds, dark.
sentences.i: He feeds on the flesh of hapless men and on their dark blood.
sentences.n: 'vescitur' is a deponent verb, and 'vescor' takes the ablative (here 'visceribus… et sanguine'), not the accusative. 'viscera' means the soft parts of the body, flesh and entrails. 'miserorum' is a masculine genitive plural used as a noun, 'of the wretched ones'. 'atro' (black, dark) agrees with 'sanguine'; 'ater' is the epic word for blood and death. In Odyssey 9 the Cyclops eats the men raw, 'like a lion', leaving nothing. This is the ordinary horror of the epic, told by an eyewitness.

sentences.t:
Vidi egomet, duo de numero cum corpora nostro
prensa manu magna, medio resupinus in antro,
frangeret ad saxum, sanieque aspersa natarent
limina;
sentences.l:
I saw it myself, when two from our number bodies
seized in his great hand, lying back in the midst of the cave,
he dashed against the rock, and with gore sprinkled swam
the thresholds;
sentences.i: I saw it with my own eyes: he lay on his back in the middle of the cave and seized two of our number in his great hand and dashed them against the rock, and the threshold, spattered with gore, swam in blood;
sentences.n: 'Vidi egomet' — '-met' strengthens 'ego', 'I myself', since he vouches as an eyewitness. 'cum… frangeret… natarent' — 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctive, 'when… he was dashing… were swimming', in narration of past time. 'duo… corpora' — 'duo' is the accusative of 'duo' ('two') and 'corpora' is the object of 'frangeret'; 'prensa' (perfect passive participle of 'prendo', 'seized') agrees with 'corpora'; 'de numero nostro' is a partitive phrase, 'out of our number'. 'resupinus' ('thrown on his back') describes the giant, lying at his ease. 'sanie aspersa' — 'aspersa', 'sprinkled', agrees with 'limina'; 'limina' is a poetic plural for the one threshold of the cave. The scene follows Odyssey 9, where the Cyclops dashes the men to the ground like puppies. 'natarent' is vivid: the floor 'swam'.

sentences.t:
vidi atro cum membra fluentia tabo
manderet, et tepidi tremerent sub dentibus artus.
sentences.l:
I saw, when the limbs dripping with black gore
he chewed, and quivered, warm, beneath his teeth, the joints.
sentences.i: I saw him chew the limbs as they ran with dark corruption, and the warm joints quiver beneath his teeth.
sentences.n: 'vidi' repeats at the head of the clause (anaphora): the eyewitness insists. 'cum… manderet… tremerent' — the same 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctive. 'tabo' is an ablative, 'with gore, corruption' (the foul fluid of a body), with 'atro' ('black'); 'fluentia' (neuter plural participle) agrees with 'membra'. 'artus' is the nominative plural of the fourth-declension noun 'artus' ('joints, limbs') and the subject of 'tremerent'; the word order puts it last in the line, and the quivering of living flesh is the worst of the picture.

sentences.t: Haud impune quidem;
sentences.l: Not unpunished, indeed;
sentences.i: But he did not do it unpunished;
sentences.n: 'Haud impune' is a litotes ('not unpunished', i.e. 'with punishment'). 'quidem' ('indeed') marks the turn: he has described the crime, and now the retribution begins.

sentences.t:
nec talia passus Ulixes,
oblitusve sui est Ithacus discrimine tanto.
sentences.l:
nor such things did Ulysses suffer,
or forgetful of himself was the Ithacan in so great a danger.
sentences.i: Ulysses did not endure such things, and the man of Ithaca did not forget himself in so great a peril.
sentences.n: 'nec talia passus (est) Ulixes' — 'passus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'patior', and 'est' is supplied from the next clause, 'oblitusve sui est': the one 'est' serves both. '-ve' ('or') continues the negative of 'nec': 'nor… or'. 'sui' is the genitive of 'se' with 'oblitus' ('forgetful of himself'), since 'obliviscor' takes the genitive of the thing forgotten. 'Ithacus' is 'the man of Ithaca'; it stands for Ulysses without his name. 'Ulixes' is Greenough's spelling of 'Ulysses'. 'discrimine tanto' is an ablative of circumstance, 'in so great a crisis'.

sentences.t:
Nam simul expletus dapibus vinoque sepultus
cervicem inflexam posuit, iacuitque per antrum
immensus, saniem eructans et frusta cruento
per somnum commixta mero,
sentences.l:
For as soon as, filled with feasts and buried in wine,
his neck bent he laid down, and he lay through the cave
huge, belching gore and scraps with bloody
in sleep mingled wine,
sentences.i: For as soon as he was gorged with his feast and sunk in wine, he laid down his bent neck and lay huge across the cave, belching gore and scraps of meat mixed with the bloody wine as he slept,
sentences.n: 'simul' stands for 'simul ac', 'as soon as', with the perfect 'posuit', 'iacuit'. 'expletus' and 'sepultus' are perfect passive participles, 'filled' and 'buried' (the second a metaphor for the heaviness of drunken sleep). 'cervicem inflexam' — the neck bent over. 'immensus' is predicative, 'lay huge'. 'saniem eructans' — 'eructo' is 'belch up'. 'frusta… commixta cruento… mero' — 'commixta' agrees with 'frusta' (neuter plural 'scraps'), 'cruento… mero' is an ablative, 'mixed with bloody wine' (the line break separates 'cruento' from its noun). This follows Odyssey 9, where the drunk giant vomits wine and bits of human flesh as he falls asleep. The period runs on to 638.

sentences.t:
nos magna precati
numina sortitique vices,
sentences.l:
we, the great
powers having prayed to and the turns having drawn lots for,
sentences.i: we prayed to the great gods and drew lots for our turns,
sentences.n: 'precati' and 'sortiti' are perfect participles of the deponents 'precor' and 'sortior', and they have an active sense ('having prayed', 'having drawn lots'). 'magna numina' — 'numen' is a god's power, 'the great divinities'. 'sortiti vices' — they cast lots for the order in which each would act. In Odyssey 9 Ulysses' men draw lots for who will help him drive the stake into the eye. The main verb 'fundimur' comes next.

sentences.t:
una undique circum
fundimur, et telo lumen terebramus acuto,—
ingens, quod torva solum sub fronte latebat,
Argolici clipei aut Phoebeae lampadis instar,—
et tandem laeti sociorum ulciscimur umbras.
sentences.l:
together from all sides around
we pour, and with a weapon the eye we bore through, sharp, —
huge, which alone beneath his grim brow lay hidden,
of an Argive shield or of the Phoebean lamp the likeness, —
and at last glad we avenge the ghosts of our comrades.
sentences.i: together we pour round him from every side and bore out his eye with a keen point — a huge eye, the only one, lying hidden under his grim brow, like an Argive shield or the lamp of Phoebus — and at last, rejoicing, we avenge the shades of our friends.
sentences.n: 'una undique circum fundimur' — 'fundimur' is passive in form with a middle sense, 'we pour ourselves', and 'una' is an adverb, 'together'. 'lumen' means the eye (as often in poetry); 'terebramus' is 'we bore through', as a carpenter drills (in Odyssey 9 the stake is twisted in the eye like a shipwright's drill). 'telo… acuto' is an ablative of means. The dashes bracket a description of the eye: 'ingens' agrees with 'lumen', and 'quod… latebat' is a relative clause, 'which lay hidden'. 'instar' is an indeclinable noun that takes a genitive ('the likeness, the size of'): 'Argolici clipei' is the round Greek shield, and 'Phoebeae lampadis' the lamp of Phoebus, the sun (some take it as the moon). 'ulciscimur umbras' — the dead are avenged by blood drawn; 'umbras' are the shades of the men eaten.

sentences.t:
Sed fugite, O miseri, fugite, atque ab litore funem
rumpite.
sentences.l:
But flee, O wretched ones, flee, and from the shore the cable
break.
sentences.i: But flee, unhappy men, flee, and tear your cable from the shore!
sentences.n: The repeated 'fugite… fugite' gives the cry of urgency. 'miseri' is a vocative, and 'O' is an interjection that goes with it. 'ab litore' ('from the shore') goes with 'rumpite': the cable fastens the ship to the land, and they must break it. 'funem' is the mooring-cable. Line 640 is the single word 'rumpite', one of Virgil's unfinished lines (half-lines): a short, sharp command.

sentences.t:
Nam qualis quantusque cavo Polyphemus in antro
lanigeras claudit pecudes atque ubera pressat,
centum alii curva haec habitant ad litora volgo
infandi Cyclopes, et altis montibus errant.
sentences.l:
For of what sort and how great in the hollow cave Polyphemus
the wool-bearing sheep shuts in and the udders presses,
a hundred others on these curved shores commonly
dwell, unspeakable Cyclopes, and on high mountains wander.
sentences.i: A hundred others, as huge and as terrible as the Polyphemus who pens his woolly flocks in the hollow cave and milks them, live in crowds along these curving shores, abominable Cyclopes, and roam the high mountains.
sentences.n: 'qualis quantusque… Polyphemus' — 'of what sort and how great' Polyphemus is, who shuts in his flocks and milks them; the comparison is left half-stated ('and as he is, so are a hundred others'). 'ubera pressat' — 'he presses the udders', i.e. milks. In Odyssey 9 the Cyclopes live scattered, each in his own cave, with no council; Virgil makes them a crowd of a hundred. 'volgo' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulgo' ('commonly, everywhere'); 'infandi' means 'unspeakable'. 'centum' and 'alii' both agree with 'Cyclopes'.

sentences.t:
Tertia iam lunae se cornua lumine complent,
cum vitam in silvis inter deserta ferarum
lustra domosque traho, vastosque ab rupe Cyclopas
prospicio, sonitumque pedum vocemque tremesco.
sentences.l:
The third now of the moon the horns with light fill themselves,
when life in the woods among the deserted of wild beasts
lairs and homes I drag out, and huge from a rock the Cyclopes
I look out upon, and the sound of feet and voice I tremble at.
sentences.i: Now for the third time the moon is filling her horns with light, while I pass my life in the woods, among the empty lairs and haunts of wild beasts, watching the huge Cyclopes from a rock and trembling at the sound of their feet and their voice.
sentences.n: 'Tertia iam… cornua' — 'tertia' agrees with 'cornua': the moon's horns are filling with light for the third time, so he has been alone for the better part of three months. 'se lumine complent' is reflexive, 'fill themselves with light'. 'cum… traho' — 'cum' with the present indicative, 'while I drag out'; set against the 'iam' of the first clause it means 'I have been dragging my life out'. 'deserta ferarum lustra' — 'deserta' agrees with 'lustra' ('haunts, lairs'), with 'ferarum' a genitive. 'ab rupe' is 'from a rock'. 'tremesco' is inceptive ('I begin to tremble') and takes the accusative ('sonitum… vocem'): he trembles at them.

sentences.t:
Victum infelicem, bacas lapidosaque corna,
dant rami et volsis pascunt radicibus herbae.
sentences.l:
A living wretched, berries and stony cornel-cherries,
the branches give, and with torn-up roots feed me the plants.
sentences.i: The boughs give me a wretched living, berries and stony cornel-cherries, and the plants feed me with roots I tear from the ground.
sentences.n: 'Victum infelicem' — 'victus' (fourth declension) is 'food, a living', and the accusative is an object of 'dant', with 'bacas lapidosaque corna'. 'corna' is the neuter plural of 'cornum', the cornel-cherry, which has a hard stone. 'volsis' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulsis': the roots are 'pulled up'. 'pascunt' has 'me' understood as its object, and its subject is 'herbae', 'the plants'. There is no model for this in Homer: the castaway on the hostile shore is Virgil's own.

sentences.t:
Omnia conlustrans, hanc primum ad litora classem
conspexi venientem.
sentences.l:
Everything scanning, this first to these shores fleet
I sighted coming.
sentences.i: Scanning everything around me, I caught sight of this fleet first, as it came towards the shore.
sentences.n: 'conlustrans' is the present participle of 'conlustro' (the familiar form is 'collustro'), 'surveying all round'. 'hanc primum… classem' — 'hanc' is a pointing word, 'this fleet here' (the speaker gestures to their ships); 'primum' is an adverb, 'first'. 'conspexi venientem' — 'venientem' is a present participle agreeing with 'classem', 'coming'.

sentences.t:
Huic me, quaecumque fuisset,
addixi:
sentences.l:
To this, whatever it might be,
I gave myself over:
sentences.i: To it, whatever it might prove to be, I gave myself up:
sentences.n: 'addixi' is the perfect of 'addico', 'assign, hand over' (a law-court word for adjudging a person or thing to someone); here he has handed himself over. 'quaecumque fuisset' — an indefinite relative clause with the pluperfect subjunctive, 'whatever it might turn out to have been' (the subjunctive gives his thought at the time). The colon introduces the reason.

sentences.t: satis est gentem effugisse nefandam.
sentences.l: enough it is the race to have escaped, accursed.
sentences.i: it is enough to have escaped that accursed race.
sentences.n: 'satis est… effugisse' — 'satis est' is impersonal, and the perfect infinitive 'effugisse' is its subject ('to have escaped is enough'). 'gentem… nefandam' — 'nefandus' is 'not to be spoken', 'accursed'. The word order puts 'nefandam' last, as a hard closing word.

sentences.t: Vos animam hanc potius quocumque absumite leto.”
sentences.l: You this life rather by whatever death consume.”
sentences.i: You, rather, take this life of mine, by whatever death you will.”
sentences.n: 'Vos' is stressed: the Trojans, against the Cyclopes. 'animam hanc' is 'this life of mine', and 'potius' means 'rather' than leaving him to the Cyclopes. 'quocumque… leto' — 'letum' (death) is an ablative of means, 'by any death whatever'. 'absumite' is the imperative of 'absumo', 'use up, destroy'. The closing mark ” ends the speech that began at 613; from the next line Aeneas is again the narrator.

sentences.t:
Vix ea fatus erat, summo cum monte videmus
ipsum inter pecudes vasta se mole moventem
pastorem Polyphemum et litora nota petentem,
monstrum horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum.
sentences.l:
Scarcely these things had he said, when on the mountain-top we see
himself among the flocks with vast bulk moving himself,
the shepherd Polyphemus, and the known shores seeking,
a monster dreadful, shapeless, huge, from whom the light was taken.
sentences.i: He had scarcely finished speaking when we see, on the mountain's crest, the shepherd Polyphemus himself, moving among his flocks with his vast bulk and making for the shores he knows, a dreadful monster, shapeless, huge, robbed of his eye.
sentences.n: Greenough begins a new paragraph here. 'Vix ea fatus erat… cum… videmus' — 'fatus erat' is the pluperfect of the deponent 'for', and the 'cum' clause with the present 'videmus' is the sudden event that interrupts ('scarcely… when'); 'cum' is held back to third place. 'summo… monte' — 'summus' means 'the top of', so 'on the mountain top'. 'ipsum… pastorem Polyphemum' — the object of 'videmus', with two participles ('moventem', 'petentem') agreeing; 'se moventem' is reflexive, 'moving himself'. 'cui lumen ademptum (est)' is a relative clause with a dative of the person deprived, 'from whom the eye was taken'.

sentences.t: Trunca manu pinus regit et vestigia firmat;
sentences.l: A lopped pine in his hand guides him and his steps steadies;
sentences.i: A lopped pine in his hand guides him and steadies his steps;
sentences.n: 'Trunca manu pinus' — 'pinus' is a feminine fourth-declension noun, nominative here, and 'trunca' ('stripped of its branches') agrees with it; 'manu' goes with the pine or with 'regit', 'in/by his hand'. The Latin Library prints 'manum', which changes the construction; Greenough's 'manu' is kept. In Odyssey 9 the blinded Cyclops gropes about with his hands; the pine staff is Virgil's. 'regit' ('guides') and 'firmat' ('steadies') are the pine's two services to a blind man.

sentences.t:
lanigerae comitantur oves—ea sola voluptas
solamenque mali.
sentences.l:
the wool-bearing sheep accompany him — that his sole pleasure
and solace of the trouble.
sentences.i: his woolly sheep go with him — the one pleasure left to him, and the relief of his suffering.
sentences.n: 'lanigerae… oves' — 'laniger' (wool-bearing) is a poetic compound. The pronoun 'ea' is feminine, attracted to the gender of the predicate noun 'voluptas' ('that is his only pleasure'), as 'haec meta' at 714. 'solamen' is a second predicate noun, joined by '-que', and 'mali' is a genitive, 'the solace of his ill'. Line 661, 'solamenque mali', is one of Virgil's unfinished half-lines. The sheep are what is left to a blind man, and the poet gives him a moment of pity.

sentences.t:
Postquam altos tetigit fluctus et ad aequora venit,
luminis effossi fluidum lavit inde cruorem,
dentibus infrendens gemitu, graditurque per aequor
iam medium, necdum fluctus latera ardua tinxit.
sentences.l:
After the deep waves he touched and to the seas came,
of the eye dug out the flowing blood he washes from there,
grinding his teeth with a groan, and he walks through the sea
now middle, nor yet had the waves his lofty flanks wetted.
sentences.i: When he has reached the deep water and come down to the sea, he washes from his torn-out eye the blood that runs from it, grinding his teeth and groaning, and wades out into the middle of the sea, though the waves have not yet wet his towering sides.
sentences.n: 'Postquam' takes the perfect indicative ('tetigit', 'venit'); the metre needs a short a in 'lavit', which makes it the present of 'lavo' ('he washes'), a historic present like 'graditur'. 'altos fluctus' — 'altus' can mean 'deep' or 'high'; here the deep water. 'luminis effossi' — a genitive of the eye 'dug out' ('effossi' is a perfect passive participle). 'fluidum… cruorem' — 'fluidus' is 'flowing'. 'dentibus infrendens' — 'infrendo' is 'gnash', and 'gemitu' is an ablative of manner. 'graditurque per aequor iam medium' — 'medium' agrees with 'aequor', 'through the now middle sea'. 'necdum… tinxit' — the perfect with 'necdum' means 'has not yet wetted', and the point is how huge he is: he wades far out and the water still hardly reaches his sides.

sentences.t:
Nos procul inde fugam trepidi celerare, recepto
supplice sic merito, tacitique incidere funem;
sentences.l:
We far from there flight, trembling, to hasten, having received
the suppliant, thus deserving, and silent to cut the cable;
sentences.i: Far from that place, trembling, we hasten our flight, having taken aboard the suppliant, who had earned it so well, and in silence we cut the cable;
sentences.n: 'celerare' and 'incidere' are historic infinitives, standing for imperfect or perfect verbs with a nominative subject ('nos… trepidi… taciti'): a quick, vivid way to narrate a hurried series of actions. 'recepto supplice' is an ablative absolute, 'the suppliant having been received'. 'sic merito' — 'merito' is the perfect participle of 'mereor' agreeing with 'supplice', 'who had so deserved (it)'. 'procul inde' — 'inde' means 'from there'.

sentences.t: vertimus et proni certantibus aequora remis.
sentences.l: we turn over, and, bending forward, with straining oars the seas.
sentences.i: and, bending forward, we sweep the sea with oars that strive together.
sentences.n: 'vertimus aequora' — the sea is 'turned over' by the oars, as a field by a plough; this is a poetic phrase for rowing hard. 'proni' agrees with the subject, 'leaning forward' at the oars. 'certantibus remis' — an ablative of means; the oars 'strive' (the rowers vie in effort).

sentences.t: Sensit, et ad sonitum vocis vestigia torsit;
sentences.l: He felt, and toward the sound of the voice his steps he turned;
sentences.i: He sensed it, and turned his steps towards the sound of our voices;
sentences.n: 'Sensit' has no object expressed: the Cyclops perceives the Trojans. 'ad sonitum vocis' — 'vocis' is a collective singular, 'the sound of voices'. 'vestigia torsit' — 'torqueo' means 'turn, twist'. The giant is guided by sound alone, as a blind man must be.

sentences.t:
verum ubi nulla datur dextra adfectare potestas,
nec potis Ionios fluctus aequare sequendo,
sentences.l:
but when no power is given by his right hand to lay hold,
nor able the Ionian waves to match in pursuing,
sentences.i: but when no power is given him to seize us with his hand, and he is unable to match the Ionian waves in pursuit,
sentences.n: 'verum ubi' ('but when') with the present 'datur'. 'dextra' is an ablative, 'with his right hand', and 'adfectare' (Greenough's spelling; the familiar form is 'affectare') is 'strive to reach, lay hold of', an infinitive depending on 'potestas'. 'nec potis' — 'potis' is an indeclinable adjective meaning 'able', with 'est' left out. 'Ionios fluctus' are the Ionian waters off the east coast of Sicily. 'aequare sequendo' — 'aequare' is 'to match, come level with', and 'sequendo' is a gerund in the ablative of means: he cannot match the waves by following. In Odyssey 9 Polyphemus hurls rocks at the ship, and Virgil gives him a roar instead.

sentences.t:
clamorem immensum tollit, quo pontus et omnes
contremuere undae, penitusque exterrita tellus
Italiae, curvisque immugiit Aetna cavernis.
sentences.l:
a shout huge he raises, at which the sea and all
the waves trembled, and deeply terrified the land
of Italy, and bellowed Etna with its winding caverns.
sentences.i: he lets out an enormous cry, at which the sea and all its waves shook, and the land of Italy was shaken to its depths, and Etna bellowed through her winding caverns.
sentences.n: 'quo' is a relative pronoun in the ablative of cause, referring to 'clamorem' ('at which'). 'contremuere' is for 'contremuerunt'. 'penitusque exterrita tellus Italiae' — a verb ('est' or 'contremuit') is understood, with 'exterrita' a participle in agreement, 'the land of Italy, terrified to its depths'. 'curvis… cavernis' is an ablative (of means or place), 'through her winding caverns'. 'immugiit' ('bellowed') is the verb for cattle: the mountain roars back like a bull.

sentences.t:
At genus e silvis Cyclopum et montibus altis
excitum ruit ad portus et litora complent.
sentences.l:
But the race out of the woods of the Cyclopes and from the high mountains
roused rushes to the harbours, and the shores they fill.
sentences.i: But the race of the Cyclopes, roused from the woods and the high mountains, rushes down to the harbours and fills the shore.
sentences.n: Greenough begins a new paragraph here. 'genus… Cyclopum' — 'Cyclopum' is the ordinary genitive plural of the third-declension 'Cyclops'. 'genus' is a collective noun, so the verb begins in the singular, 'ruit', and ends in the plural, 'complent', a change of number by sense. 'e silvis… et montibus altis' — 'e' serves both nouns. 'excitum' is a perfect passive participle, 'roused'. In Odyssey 9 the other Cyclopes come to Polyphemus's cave at his cry and ask what is wrong; here they come too late.

sentences.t:
Cernimus adstantis nequiquam lumine torvo
Aetnaeos fratres, caelo capita alta ferentis,
concilium horrendum:
sentences.l:
We see standing by in vain with grim eye
the Aetnaean brothers, to the sky their heads high bearing,
a council dreadful:
sentences.i: We see them standing there to no purpose, glaring with their one grim eye, the brothers from Etna, raising their lofty heads to the sky — a dreadful assembly:
sentences.n: 'adstantis' and 'ferentis' are Greenough's accusative plurals in '-is' (you'll see this constantly); they agree with 'fratres'. 'nequiquam' means 'in vain': they stand and can only glare. 'lumine torvo' — an ablative of manner or description; the singular 'lumine' points to the one eye each has. 'Aetnaeos fratres' — brothers of Polyphemus, from Etna. 'concilium horrendum' is in apposition to 'fratres' ('as a dreadful assembly'); a 'concilium' is an assembly, a grim word to use of giants. The colon introduces a simile.

sentences.t:
quales cum vertice celso
aeriae quercus, aut coniferae cyparissi
constiterunt, silva alta Iovis, lucusve Dianae.
sentences.l:
such as when on a high peak
airy oaks, or cone-bearing cypresses
have taken their stand, a high wood of Jove, or a grove of Diana.
sentences.i: They are like lofty oaks or cone-bearing cypresses when they stand together on a high summit, a tall wood of Jove or a grove of Diana.
sentences.n: 'quales cum… constiterunt' — 'quales' is a relative adjective of comparison (the antecedent 'tales' is understood), and 'cum' with the perfect indicative 'constiterunt' means 'when they have taken their stand'. 'aeriae' means 'lofty, in the air'. 'coniferae cyparissi' — 'cyparissus' is a second-declension noun, feminine like most tree names, so 'cyparissi' is nominative plural with 'coniferae' agreeing. 'silva alta Iovis, lucusve Dianae' — an apposition, with the trees as 'a high wood of Jove, or a grove of Diana'. In Odyssey 9 Polyphemus is likened to a wooded peak; Virgil spreads the image over the whole race.

sentences.t:
Praecipites metus acer agit quocumque rudentis
excutere, et ventis intendere vela secundis.
sentences.l:
Headlong sharp fear drives, wherever, the ropes
to shake out, and to the winds to stretch the sails favourable.
sentences.i: Sharp fear drives us headlong to cast out the ropes, in whatever direction, and to stretch the sails to the favouring winds.
sentences.n: 'Praecipites' is an accusative plural agreeing with an understood 'nos'. 'metus acer agit… excutere… intendere' — 'ago' with infinitives, 'drives to shake, to stretch'. 'rudentis' is Greenough's accusative plural in '-is' of 'rudens', 'rope, rigging'; 'excutere rudentis' means to shake out the ropes so that the sail can run. 'quocumque' means 'in whatever direction'; the phrase is compressed. 'ventis secundis' — 'secundus' means 'following', i.e. 'favouring'.

sentences.i: But against this stand the warnings of Helenus: between Scylla and Charybdis either way lies a narrow margin from death, unless the ships hold their course;
sentences.n: 'Contra' is an adverb here, 'on the other hand'; 'iussa Heleni' are the instructions Helenus gave in the earlier part of this book, and the neuter plural subject has a plural verb, 'monent'. What they warn is in indirect speech: 'utramque viam (esse) leti discrimine parvo', 'each way is at a small distance from death'. The Latin Library prints 'utrimque', 'on both sides', with much the same sense. 'Scyllam atque Charybdin inter' — 'inter' follows its two nouns; 'Charybdin' is a Greek accusative. 'ni teneant cursus' — the subjunctive stands in indirect speech, 'unless they keep their course'. The Latin Library has 'teneam', 'unless I keep', the first person; Greenough's 'teneant' is kept and the subject is the ships' company. The Homeric model is Odyssey 12, where Circe warns Ulysses of the same pair.

sentences.t: certum est dare lintea retro.
sentences.l: it is decided to give the sails back.
sentences.i: we are resolved to turn the sails about.
sentences.n: 'certum est' is impersonal and means 'it is resolved', with an infinitive. 'dare lintea retro' — 'lintea' (linen) stands for 'sails', and the phrase is a nautical one: 'give the sails back', i.e. put about and run back the way they came. They will not enter the strait with its twin dangers.

sentences.t:
Ecce autem Boreas angusta ab sede Pelori
missus adest.
sentences.l:
Behold, however, Boreas from the narrow seat of Pelorus
sent is here.
sentences.i: And now, look, Boreas arrives, sent down from the narrow headland of Pelorus.
sentences.n: 'Ecce autem' marks a sudden change. 'Boreas' is the north wind, a Greek name. 'angusta ab sede Pelori' — 'Pelorus' (the genitive 'Pelori') is the north-eastern cape of Sicily, at the narrow strait; 'sede' is a seat or place. 'missus adest' — 'missus' means 'sent', so 'is here, sent': a favourable wind for sailing south.

sentences.t:
Vivo praetervehor ostia saxo
Pantagiae Megarosque sinus Thapsumque iacentem.
sentences.l:
With living rock I am carried past the mouths
of Pantagias and the Megarian bays and Thapsus lying low.
sentences.i: I am carried past the mouth of the Pantagias with its natural rock, past the Megarian bays and past low-lying Thapsus.
sentences.n: 'Vivo saxo' — 'living rock' is native rock, an ablative describing 'ostia' ('the mouths'). 'Pantagiae' is the Greek genitive of 'Pantagias', a small river on the east coast of Sicily. 'Megaros… sinus' — 'Megaros' is an accusative plural masculine adjective ('Megarian') agreeing with 'sinus' (fourth declension, accusative plural), the bays by Megara Hyblaea. 'Thapsum… iacentem' — Thapsus, a low peninsula that 'lies flat'. 'praetervehor' is passive in form with a middle sense and takes an accusative, 'I sail past'. From here Aeneas lists the places as the ships pass them.

sentences.t:
Talia monstrabat relegens errata retrorsus
litora Achaemenides;
sentences.l:
Such things was pointing out, retracing back
the wandered shores, Achaemenides;
sentences.i: Such were the sights Achaemenides pointed out as we coasted back along the shores he had wandered;
sentences.n: 'Talia monstrabat' — the imperfect, 'he used to point out, was pointing out'. 'relegens errata… litora' — 'relego' is 'travel over again, retrace', and 'errata' is a perfect passive participle of the intransitive 'erro', used passively of the ground covered, 'the shores wandered over'. 'retrorsus' means 'backwards', 'back along'. The semicolon sets the apposition that follows.

sentences.t: comes infelicis Ulixi.
sentences.l: companion of unlucky Ulysses.
sentences.i: that companion of unlucky Ulysses.
sentences.n: 'comes infelicis Ulixi' repeats word for word the first line of his speech (613), as if to close his story in a ring. 'comes' is in apposition to 'Achaemenides'. 'Ulixi' is the genitive of 'Ulixes' (Greenough's spelling).

sentences.t:
Sicanio praetenta sinu iacet insula contra
Plemyrium undosum;
sentences.l:
In front of the Sicanian bay stretched lies an island opposite
wave-beaten Plemyrium;
sentences.i: An island lies stretched out before the Sicanian bay, facing wave-beaten Plemyrium;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sicanio… sinu' — the Sicani were an old people of Sicily, so 'Sicanian' means Sicilian; the bay is that of Syracuse. 'praetenta' is a perfect passive participle, 'stretched before'. 'contra Plemyrium undosum' — 'contra' is a preposition with the accusative, 'opposite'. Plemyrium is a headland south of Syracuse. 'iacet insula' — the island is Ortygia.

sentences.t:
nomen dixere priores
Ortygiam.
sentences.l:
the name called the earlier ones
Ortygia.
sentences.i: men of earlier days gave it the name Ortygia.
sentences.n: 'dixere' = 'dixerunt' (the ending '-ere' for '-erunt'). 'nomen… Ortygiam' — the name is in apposition with 'Ortygiam', 'they called its name Ortygia'. 'priores' is a comparative used as a noun, 'the earlier ones, the men of old'. The island is the oldest part of Syracuse.

sentences.t:
Alpheum fama est huc Elidis amnem
occultas egisse vias subter mare; qui nunc
ore, Arethusa, tuo Siculis confunditur undis.
sentences.l:
Alpheus, the story is, hither, the river of Elis,
hidden ways drove beneath the sea; which now
at your mouth, Arethusa, with Sicilian waves is mingled.
sentences.i: The story goes that the Alpheus, a river of Elis, drove its hidden channels under the sea to this place, and that now, Arethusa, it mingles at your mouth with the Sicilian waves.
sentences.n: 'fama est' takes an accusative and infinitive, 'Alpheum… egisse', 'the tradition is that Alpheus drove'. The Alpheus is a river of Elis in the Peloponnese; the story is that it ran under the sea to join the spring Arethusa in Ortygia. 'qui' is a relative pronoun referring to 'Alpheum'. 'ore, Arethusa, tuo' — the poet addresses the spring directly (apostrophe), and 'ore' is its mouth. 'Siculis undis' is a dative (or ablative) with the compound verb 'confunditur', 'is mixed with'.

sentences.t: Iussi numina magna loci veneramur;
sentences.l: Commanded, the great divinities of the place we worship;
sentences.i: As we are bidden, we worship the great powers of the place;
sentences.n: 'Iussi' is a perfect passive participle, 'having been bidden', and Aeneas does not say by whom. 'numina magna loci' — 'numen' is a god's power, here the spirits of the place; 'loci' is a genitive. 'veneramur' is a deponent verb in the present, 'we worship'.

sentences.t:
et inde
exsupero praepingue solum stagnantis Helori.
sentences.l:
and from there
I pass beyond the very rich soil of the standing Helorus.
sentences.i: and from there I pass the rich, fat land of the Helorus, where its waters stand.
sentences.n: 'exsupero' means 'pass beyond, sail past'. 'praepingue' is 'very rich' (pinguis, fat). 'stagnantis' is a genitive singular of the present participle, agreeing with 'Helori': a river whose waters stand in pools and marsh. 'Helorus' is a river of south-eastern Sicily.

sentences.t:
Hinc altas cautes proiectaque saxa Pachyni
radimus,
sentences.l:
From here the high crags and the projecting rocks of Pachynus
we skim,
sentences.i: From there we skim past the high crags and jutting rocks of Pachynus,
sentences.n: 'radimus' means 'we scrape, graze', that is, we sail close along the coast. 'proiecta saxa' — 'proiecta' is a perfect passive participle, 'thrown forward, jutting'. 'Pachyni' is the genitive of Pachynus, the south-eastern point of Sicily.

sentences.t:
et fatis numquam concessa moveri
adparet Camerina procul campique Geloi,
immanisque Gela fluvii cognomine dicta.
sentences.l:
and by the fates never allowed to be moved
appears Camerina far off and the Geloan fields,
and huge Gela, from the name of the river called.
sentences.i: and far off appear Camerina, which the fates have never allowed to be disturbed, and the Geloan plains, and vast Gela, named for its river.
sentences.n: 'fatis numquam concessa moveri' — 'concessa' is a perfect passive participle, 'allowed', with a passive infinitive 'moveri' ('to be moved'), a poetic construction; 'fatis' is the dative of the agent, 'by the fates'. The reference is, as ancient commentators say, to an oracle forbidding the draining of the marsh by Camerina. 'campi Geloi' — 'Geloi' is a Greek adjective ('Geloan') agreeing with 'campi'. 'immanisque Gela fluvii cognomine dicta' — 'cognomine' is an ablative of cause, 'named from the river'. 'adparet' is Greenough's spelling of 'apparet'.

sentences.t:
Arduus inde Acragas ostentat maxuma longe
moenia, magnanimum quondam generator equorum;
sentences.l:
Towering then Acragas shows greatest from afar
its walls, of high-spirited horses once the breeder;
sentences.i: Then lofty Acragas shows its mighty walls from afar, once the breeder of spirited horses;
sentences.n: 'Acragas' is the Greek name of Agrigentum (the city and the river). 'maxuma' is Greenough's spelling of 'maxima'. 'magnanimum… equorum' — 'magnanimum' is the old genitive plural for 'magnanimorum' (you'll see this constantly, as with 'superum'). 'generator' is 'a breeder'; the city was famous for its horses. 'quondam' means 'once'.

sentences.t:
teque datis linquo ventis, palmosa Selinus,
et vada dura lego saxis Lilybeia caecis.
sentences.l:
and you, with the winds given, I leave, palm-bearing Selinus,
and the shallows hard with hidden rocks of Lilybaeum I skim.
sentences.i: With the winds granted me, I leave you behind, Selinus of the palms, and skirt the shoals of Lilybaeum, perilous with hidden rocks.
sentences.n: 'te… palmosa Selinus' — an apostrophe to the city, with a vocative that has the same form as the nominative; 'palmosa' means 'rich in palms'. 'datis ventis' is an ablative absolute, 'the winds being granted'. 'lego' means 'I skim, sail along'. 'vada dura… saxis… caecis' — 'dura' means 'dangerous', and 'saxis caecis' is an ablative of cause or description, 'hidden rocks' (rocks that cannot be seen). 'Lilybeia' is the adjective of Lilybaeum, a cape on the west of Sicily.

sentences.t:
Hinc Drepani me portus et inlaetabilis ora
accipit.
sentences.l:
From here of Drepanum me the harbour and joyless shore
receives.
sentences.i: From there the harbour of Drepanum and its joyless shore take me in.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Drepani' is the genitive of Drepanum (modern Trapani), on the west coast of Sicily. The verb 'accipit' is singular with two subjects ('portus… ora'), agreeing with the nearer; this is regular. 'inlaetabilis' means 'joyless', formed on 'laetor' (Greenough's 'in-' keeps the unassimilated prefix). The place name will be important: this is where Anchises dies.

sentences.t:
Hic, pelagi tot tempestatibus actis,
heu genitorem, omnis curae casusque levamen,
amitto Anchisen:
sentences.l:
Here, of the sea so many storms having been driven through,
alas, my father, of all care and misfortune the relief,
I lose Anchises:
sentences.i: Here, after the sea's many storms have been passed through, alas, I lose my father Anchises, the comfort of every care and every mischance:
sentences.n: 'pelagi tot tempestatibus actis' — an ablative absolute, 'so many storms of the sea having been driven through'. The Latin Library prints 'actus', which would make Aeneas himself 'driven' by the storms; Greenough's 'actis' is kept. 'omnis curae casusque levamen' — 'omnis' is a genitive singular here (not an accusative plural), 'relief of every care and mischance'. 'genitorem… Anchisen' — the common noun is placed first, with 'heu' in the middle, and the name delayed to the end of the line, where it comes with a weight. 'Anchisen' is a Greek accusative. Aeneas's story of Troy and of the wandering ends in the loss of his father.

sentences.t:
hic me, pater optume, fessum
deseris, heu, tantis nequiquam erepte periclis!
sentences.l:
here me, best father, weary
you leave, alas, from so great dangers in vain rescued!
sentences.i: Here, best of fathers, you leave me, weary as I am — you, alas, delivered from such great perils for no purpose!
sentences.n: Aeneas turns to address his dead father directly (apostrophe). 'optume' is Greenough's spelling of 'optime', the vocative of the superlative. 'hic' repeats 'hic' of the line before. 'erepte' is a vocative of the perfect passive participle, 'you who were rescued', agreeing with the 'pater' addressed; 'periclis' is an ablative of separation, 'from perils' (Aeneas had carried Anchises out of burning Troy). 'nequiquam' means 'in vain'.

sentences.t:
Nec vates Helenus, cum multa horrenda moneret,
hos mihi praedixit luctus, non dira Celaeno.
sentences.l:
Nor the seer Helenus, when many dreadful things he was warning,
these to me foretold griefs, nor dread Celaeno.
sentences.i: Neither the seer Helenus, though he warned me of many terrors, nor dread Celaeno foretold me these griefs.
sentences.n: 'cum multa horrenda moneret' — 'cum' with the subjunctive is concessive, 'although'; 'multa horrenda' is 'many dreadful things'. 'non dira Celaeno' — the verb 'praedixit' is understood: 'Celaeno did not foretell them either'. Celaeno is the Harpy who prophesied to the Trojans earlier in this book. 'luctus' is an accusative plural of the fourth declension. Neither prophet had told Aeneas that he would lose his father.

sentences.t: Hic labor extremus, longarum haec meta viarum.
sentences.l: Here toil the last, of long journeys this the goal.
sentences.i: This was my last toil, this the end of my long journeys.
sentences.n: A sentence without a verb ('est' is understood). 'Hic labor extremus' — 'hic' is 'here' or 'this', and the ellipsis gives the tone of finality. 'haec meta' — 'haec' is attracted to the gender of the noun 'meta' ('this is the goal'), as 'ea' was in 660. 'meta' is the turning-post of a racecourse, so 'the end of the course'. The line closes Aeneas's account: the end of the story he is telling Dido.

sentences.t: Hinc me digressum vestris deus adpulit oris.
sentences.l: From here me, having departed, to your shores a god drove.
sentences.i: When I had left that place, a god brought me to your shores.
sentences.n: 'digressum' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'digredior' and agrees with 'me'. 'vestris oris' is a dative of direction, 'to your shores', without a preposition, a poetic usage: Aeneas speaks to Dido and the Carthaginians. 'deus' is left unnamed. 'adpulit' is Greenough's spelling of 'appulit'. 'Hinc' is the place, Drepanum.

sentences.t:
Sic pater Aeneas intentis omnibus unus
fata renarrabat divom, cursusque docebat.
sentences.l:
Thus father Aeneas, all being intent, alone
the fates of the gods was telling again, and his courses was teaching.
sentences.i: So father Aeneas, while all listened intently, alone went back over the decrees of heaven and set out the course of his voyages.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. The narrator speaks again; Aeneas has told the story since the beginning of Book II. 'intentis omnibus' is an ablative absolute, 'all being attentive'. 'unus' means 'alone', 'by himself': one voice among a silent company. 'fata divom' — 'divom' is the old genitive plural of 'divus' (you'll see this constantly: 'divom', 'virum', 'superum'), 'the fates (decrees) of the gods'. 'renarrabat' and 'docebat' are imperfects of continued action, 'was relating' and 'was setting forth'; 'cursus' is an accusative plural, 'voyages'.

sentences.t: Conticuit tandem, factoque hic fine quievit.
sentences.l: He fell silent at last, and, an end here made, he rested.
sentences.i: At last he fell silent, and, having made an end there, he rested.
sentences.n: 'Conticuit' is the perfect, 'fell silent', and it closes the frame that opened when all the company fell silent to hear him. 'facto… fine' is an ablative absolute, 'an end having been made'; 'hic' means 'at this point'. 'quievit' means 'rested, was still'. It is the last line of Book III.
